item.title: CCTV at Hong Kong malls and the police SmartView programme
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Hong Kong's Secretary for Security said in an interview on 18 October that some CCTV cameras at private shopping malls will be connected to the police SmartView programme, with talks in their final stage. He also said the public may not need to be told separately, and in February said that third-party connections are one-way and that footage on the government system is generally kept for 31 days. People travelling to Hong Kong for leisure or business may be caught on camera in public areas of malls, and places outside Hong Kong are not affected. According to Hong Kong media reports, facial recognition is being piloted in parts of the system.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 23 sources, including Security Bureau, Hong Kong Police Force, Hong Kong Police Force, Legislative Council Secretariat

Hong Kong's Secretary for Security said in a television interview on 18 October that some CCTV cameras at private shopping malls will be connected to the Hong Kong Police Force's SmartView programme, and that talks with the malls had reached their final stage. He did not name the malls. According to HK01, he also said the public may not need to be told that cameras have been connected, depending on each mall's practice. People travelling to Hong Kong for leisure or business may appear on connected cameras when passing through public areas of malls, and places outside Hong Kong are not affected.

According to a paper the Security Bureau and the police submitted to the Legislative Council in February, SmartView is a government-led programme to install CCTV in public places with high crime rates and heavy pedestrian flow, with aims including safeguarding national security, preventing crime, assisting investigations and managing crowds. The first phase was completed at the end of 2025, with about 5,000 cameras installed by the police and about 6,000 cameras of other government departments and organisations connected. According to the paper, about 60,000 cameras are planned across the city by 2028 and about 6,500 more between 2028 and 2031, and from its launch in April 2024 to January 2026 the programme helped the police detect 899 cases. According to The Collective HK, the Legislative Council's Finance Committee approved funding of about HK$4.06 billion on 27 March.

The same paper lists AI functions including crowd size estimation and number plate recognition, and the Secretary told the Legislative Council in February that facial recognition would be added so the system could track suspects across cameras automatically. According to Dim Sum Daily, he said in the 18 October interview that facial recognition is being piloted in parts of the system. The Commissioner of Police said in an interview in February that the public would be informed before it is deployed. According to Sing Tao Daily, the Commissioner hopes to introduce it by 2027 at the latest, with the timing depending on conditions including a legal framework.

According to Hong Kong Free Press, the Secretary said that whether police can see live footage or only download it afterwards would depend on the location's crime risk. He told the Legislative Council in February that third-party connections are one-way, so third parties cannot obtain data from the system. He also said footage on the government system is generally kept for 31 days and then deleted automatically, unless a designated officer of a higher rank decides on other use. On the arrangements for malls, Dim Sum Daily reported the Secretary as saying in October that they would follow each mall's existing policies.

Perspective

Our inference is that once cameras are connected, police could view or retrieve through the system footage that each mall previously stored on its own. Based on the Secretary's description to the Legislative Council in February, adding facial recognition would turn the search for a suspect from reviewing footage clip by clip by hand into automatic tracking across cameras. Under the October 2025 CCTV guidance from Hong Kong's Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD), facial identification and tracking of individuals are not normally expected by the public, so their use must be supported by strong justification.

In 2019 the Hong Kong government disabled three functions on smart lampposts over privacy concerns, and in 2020 a technical advisory committee recommended more privacy-friendly technologies in place of the lampposts' cameras and Bluetooth detectors. As of 23 October, the places listed on the police SmartView page for installing cameras include ordinary lampposts and smart lampposts.

According to Hong Kong Free Press, the Secretary said that many malls already display signs warning of recording, so the public may not need to be told separately that cameras are connected to the police system. The notice for third-party cameras shown on the police SmartView page is posted at the discretion of the property owner. Under the PCPD's guidance, notices should name the data user operating the system and the specific purpose of the surveillance.

According to the minutes of the Legislative Council Panel on Security's February meeting, members raised concerns about how the cameras would safeguard the public's privacy and personal data security, and in the same minutes members supported proceeding with the second and third phases. According to a Hong Kong Free Press report from October 2025, Hong Kong had no rules on how law enforcement could use AI, and the PCPD had declined to tell AFP whether it had been consulted. As of 23 October, we could not find any public response from the PCPD to SmartView, nor a legal framework specific to facial recognition.

According to the police SmartView page, cameras installed under the programme capture only public places, and an independent consultancy was commissioned to conduct a privacy impact assessment. There is no mention on the page of whether third-party cameras also capture only public places or are covered by that assessment. The Commissioner of Police said in a February interview that the government is working on a legal framework for facial recognition. The Secretary told the Legislative Council in February that the AI analysis then under discussion all took place after a crime and would not systematically intrude on privacy, and that the Department of Justice and the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data had been consulted.

People caught on camera, including visitors, can use the form specified by the PCPD to make a data access request to the organisation holding the footage, and requests to the police can be made at a police station, by post or online. The organisation must respond within 40 days and may ask for proof of identity and charge a fee, and the form's identity field also accepts a passport number. According to the PCPD's practical guide, data held for preventing or detecting crime can be exempted under section 58 of the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance where giving access would be likely to prejudice that purpose. According to the same guide, a data user must have sufficient evidence that the data is held for these purposes, and a mere general assertion is not enough.

We, a community based in Taiwan, compared three other places in Asia on the same points as Hong Kong, using laws we read on 23 October. On who can draw on cameras that police do not own, Taiwan's Police Power Exercise Act lets police collect data with existing recording equipment in public places or places open to the public, which we read as including malls, where crime is frequent or reasonably expected, though we did not check whether privately owned cameras are covered. In mainland China, shopping centres are among the places covered by the State Council's regulations on public security video systems, in force since 1 April 2025, and state organs retrieving that footage for law enforcement must follow the authority and procedures set by laws and administrative regulations.

In South Korea, those with proper authority, such as malls, may install cameras in public places for facility safety and management under the Personal Information Protection Act. Under Article 18(2) of the same act, they may provide footage to others with the person's separate consent or where another law makes special provision, unless this would unfairly infringe the interests of the person or a third party. The provision on disclosure for criminal investigations (Article 18(2) item 7) applies only to public institutions, and we did not check which provisions of laws such as the Criminal Procedure Act apply.

On notices, South Korea requires signs giving the purpose and location, the area and hours filmed and a contact for the person in charge, while Taiwan's Article 10 contains no provision on notices. Mainland China's regulations require a conspicuous notice without setting its content, and its measures on facial recognition, in force since 1 June 2025, require operators to tell people beforehand, in a conspicuous way, matters such as the operator's name and contact details, the purpose and the retention period, unless laws or administrative regulations allow otherwise. For mainland China we did not check internal rules on police use of facial recognition.

On retention, according to the Secretary, footage on Hong Kong's government system is generally kept for 31 days and then deleted automatically. Mainland China's Article 17 sets a minimum for the units managing public security video systems, malls included, which must keep footage for at least 30 days before deleting what has served its purpose. Taiwan's Article 10 sets a maximum for data collected by police, which must be destroyed within one year unless needed to investigate a suspected crime or other violation. We did not check South Korea's retention rules.

Readers can weigh the programme with a few questions. First, on the effect the government wants, whether figures on cases solved will be published after malls are connected. Second, on the safeguards Legislative Council members raised, whether what is announced before facial recognition is deployed includes the legal basis and retention rules. Third, on the notices called for in the PCPD's guidance, whether connected malls let passers-by know their footage goes to the police.

Next, it is worth watching when the police announce the timing and legal framework for facial recognition, whether the connected malls are made public, and whether the PCPD responds to SmartView.

item.title: AI training and cookie rules in the EU Digital Omnibus
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 21 October, EU member states agreed the Council of the EU's position on the draft Digital Omnibus, under which the GDPR would state that personal data may be processed on the basis of "legitimate interest" to develop and operate AI, and cookies would need no consent in more cases. It is the Council's position for negotiating with the European Parliament, which had not formed its own as of 23 October. The GDPR applies to personal data processed by businesses established in the EU, and also protects people in the EU who are offered services or whose behaviour is monitored by businesses outside it; otherwise, readers outside the EU are not directly affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 24 sources, including Council of the European Union, EuropaWire, European Commission

The permanent representatives of EU member states agreed the Council of the EU's position on the draft Digital Omnibus on 21 October, a proposal the European Commission put forward in November 2025. Under the Council's position, the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) would state that personal data may be processed to develop and operate AI on the basis of "legitimate interest", a legal basis that needs no prior consent but requires weighing the rights of the people concerned. The Council document is titled a mandate for negotiations with the European Parliament, so it is not the final law, and as of 23 October the Parliament's procedure page still read "Awaiting committee decision". The GDPR applies to personal data processed by businesses established in the EU, and also protects people in the EU who are offered services or whose behaviour is monitored by businesses outside it; otherwise, readers outside the EU are not directly affected.

Under Article 88bis of the Council's text, personal data may be processed under the GDPR's legitimate interest when developing and operating an AI system or model, with technical and organisational safeguards. The Commission's proposal listed data minimisation, enhanced transparency and an "unconditional right to object" in the article itself, and excluded cases where the rights of the people concerned override. The Council removed enhanced transparency and the overriding-rights exception from the article, and replaced the right to object with the one in Article 21 of the GDPR, which has to be based on a person's particular situation. Data minimisation and the overriding-rights balance moved to a recital (an explanatory passage before the articles that is not itself binding), and according to the same recital, developing or operating AI does not in itself constitute a legitimate interest and has to be assessed case by case.

The Commission had proposed changing the definition of personal data in Article 4(1) of the GDPR. In February the European Data Protection Board (EDPB, made up of national data protection authorities) and the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS, which oversees the EU institutions' own handling of personal data) strongly urged lawmakers not to adopt it, and the Council dropped the change. The Council added a new Article 25a, under which pseudonymised data (data in which fields that directly identify a person are replaced with codes) is not personal data for a third party that cannot identify the person.

The Commission had proposed moving the cookie rules into the GDPR, but the Council kept them in the ePrivacy Directive, which governs privacy in electronic communications, and widened the cases where no user consent is needed. The new cases include showing ads and measuring their performance based only on the content of the page being viewed, without using personal data. Under the Council's version, a site may not ask again for the same purpose for at least four months after a user refuses. The Commission's proposal set the period at six months, so under the Council's version sites can ask again sooner.

In a June letter to member state representatives, the consumer organisation BEUC supported letting browsers send consent or refusal signals automatically, and the Council did not keep that design.

Perspective

If the Council's version becomes the final law, companies could point to the article to claim legitimate interest for using personal data to develop AI, and more cookies would need no consent. The LinkedIn and Gemini settings covered further down have nothing to do with this bill and were already available as of 23 October.

Legitimate interest is one of the six legal bases in the GDPR, under which a company does not need prior consent but has to show the processing is necessary and weigh it against the rights of the people concerned. According to an EDPB opinion of December 2024, legitimate interest can in some cases be the legal basis for developing and deploying AI models. Under Article 21 of the GDPR, a person can object on grounds relating to their particular situation, and the company can continue only if it shows compelling legitimate grounds that override.

According to the explanatory memorandum to the Commission's proposal, one aim of the changes is to clarify some rules on processing data for AI training and development. Industry groups, in a letter to the Council in September on the compromise text of the time (the letter itself is undated), asked for the legal basis to be written into the articles themselves, because a recital alone would not give businesses certainty. In its October mandate, the Council placed Article 88bis in the articles themselves. In their joint opinion on the Commission's proposal in February, the EDPB and the EDPS concluded that the GDPR does not need a separate article for this, and that companies would still have to pass the same case-by-case assessment.

As of 23 October, the only public response to the text agreed in October that we found came from noyb, an Austrian privacy advocacy group. In noyb's reading of 23 October, the agreed text makes processing "in the context of AI" automatically lawful, which noyb calls a "digital expropriation" of Europeans. In a letter of 18 September on the compromise text of the time, EDRi, a coalition of European digital rights groups, wrote that the article does not make all AI-related processing automatically lawful but risks turning a case-by-case assessment into a broad legislative endorsement. In the Council's recital, developing AI does not in itself constitute a legitimate interest, and according to the Council's press release (as republished), appropriate safeguards are maintained alongside support for AI innovation.

According to the Council's press release, the definition is unchanged and the new pseudonymisation provision aims to clarify compliance requirements for organisations. noyb regards it as drastically narrowing what counts as personal data, which makes it unclear whether online tracking would still be covered by the GDPR. Under another paragraph of Article 25a, when data is passed to a third party that can identify the person, both the transfer and the later processing still count as processing personal data. According to EDRi's letter, the same pseudonymised data may be non-personal for some organisations and personal for others.

When processing relies on legitimate interest, people in the EU can object under Article 21. According to Meta's announcement of April 2025, EU users can also object through a form to their public data being used for training, and the announcement does not name the article this relies on.

As of 23 October, the generative AI training setting on LinkedIn's help page is on by default, turning it off stops only future training, and no regional limit appears on the page. According to Google's help page, checked the same day, turning off Gemini's Keep Activity and not submitting feedback keeps future chats out of AI model improvement. According to the same page, these settings do not cover using chats to produce anonymised data for improving services. Chats are still kept for 72 hours after the setting is turned off, to respond to users and protect Google, users and the public, and may be reviewed by people during that time.

We, a community based in Taiwan, compared South Korea, Japan and Taiwan on when personal data can be used for AI training without consent, and did not check the rights to object or refuse in South Korea and Japan. According to guidance the South Korean Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) published on 6 August 2025, building on its July 2024 guidance on publicly available personal information, the legal basis that can realistically be considered for collecting public personal information from the web is the legitimate interest clause in Article 15(1)6 of the Personal Information Protection Act. Under the guidance, the purpose has to be legitimate, the processing necessary, and the company's legitimate interest has to clearly override the rights of the people concerned, a threshold that also appears in the statutory clause itself. Under Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR, processing is allowed unless the interests of the people concerned override the company's, so the Korean clause puts a higher bar on the company (our comparison).

The National Assembly passed an amendment on 20 August 2026 that adds a separate route, alongside existing legal bases, under which lawfully collected personal information can be used for AI development where pseudonymised or anonymised data is not enough and there is a public or social need, with stronger safeguards and prior deliberation and resolution by the PIPC. It takes effect six months after promulgation, so it cannot take effect before February 2027. Article 88bis in the Council's text has no comparable prior review by a regulator, and Korea's existing legitimate interest clause has none either, so the comparison is with the new special route (our comparison).

Under Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information, as of 23 October consent is required, outside its exceptions, to acquire sensitive personal information such as creed, medical history or criminal record and to provide personal data to third parties. Once an amendment promulgated on 17 July 2026 takes effect, consent would no longer be needed to provide personal data to third parties or to acquire sensitive information that has been made public when the data is used only to produce statistical information, which covers AI development that can be classed as producing statistics. The conditions include publishing who is involved and what they intend to do, a written agreement between the provider and the recipient, and a ban on other uses and onward provision. The amendment takes effect in principle within two years of promulgation, and as of 23 October no date appears on the page of the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) and the implementing orders and rules are still under consideration, so we take it as not yet in force.

Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act has no provision on AI training as of 23 October. Under Article 19, a non-government entity with a specific purpose may collect data from generally available sources without consent, except for the medical, genetic and other data listed in Article 6, or where the person has a clearly greater interest to protect. Under Article 20, using data, which includes using it for training, must stay within the specific purpose of collection, and under Article 3, people can ask for collection, processing or use to stop and for their data to be deleted. Under Article 14 of the AI Basic Act, promulgated in January 2026, the authorities in charge of each sector are to work with the personal data protection authority to avoid unnecessary collection, processing or use of personal data in AI research and applications.

Readers can compare the version the European Parliament eventually forms with the Council's using a few questions. First, once legitimate interest is written into the article, do companies gain more certainty, and do data protection authorities still review case by case. Second, can people actually use the right to object, and would the new pseudonymisation rule take online tracking outside the GDPR. Third, would people see fewer cookie consent banners, one of the effects the Commission's proposal set out to achieve.

item.title: Weekly brief, 2026 week 43
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Five stories and follow-ups from 1 to 22 October: progress on Session's Protocol v2, the development of Thunderbird for iOS, CryptPad 2026.10.0, PipePipe 5.5.0, and docket activity in a civil rights suit against two Florida state troopers in the US.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 12 sources, including Session, Thunderbird, GitHub

This issue collects five stories, three of them follow-ups to earlier articles, covering 1 to 22 October.

Progress on Session Protocol v2

Session, a messaging app you can register for without a phone number, described the progress of its new Protocol v2 in a blog post on 13 October. Forward secrecy for one-to-one messages (past messages stay unreadable even if keys leak) and post-quantum encryption (encryption designed to resist attacks by future quantum computers) have been implemented in the shared library libsession, and the post-quantum part will use a hybrid design that combines a post-quantum algorithm with the current one. As of 23 October, the apps had shipped only forward-compatibility handling: a message in the v2 format shows up as a placeholder asking the user to update, and the apps cannot yet send v2 messages.

According to the same post, device groups (joining, removal and membership management) are still in development, and the migration plan for existing accounts is still being designed. An account can only switch to v2 once all its linked devices support it, and the switch may then need to be confirmed manually. Session's fundraising post of 8 October states that v2 does not yet have a release date.

In another post on 19 October, Session wrote that Session Router 1.1, the onion routing layer future versions of Session will use to connect to the node network, has added forward secrecy and a post-quantum key exchange. Node operators can choose whether to upgrade for now, and Session recommends that they do. According to the v2 post, Session Router will later become the main transport layer for v2.

Development of Thunderbird for iOS

Thunderbird, the open-source email software, set out the design direction for its iPhone version on its official blog on 1 October, writing that the goal is a first version ready for community testing within the next few months. As of 23 October, the app was not on the App Store, and the GitHub repository's description says the project is in early development and not yet usable. On 23 October, the public TestFlight page (Apple's platform for distributing beta apps) showed the beta as full.

According to the team's replies in the post's comments, iCloud mail accounts can sign in over IMAP with the account password. As of 18 October, sign-in for Google and Microsoft accounts was still an open work item on GitHub. As of 23 October, we found no mention of OpenPGP (the standard for end-to-end encrypted email) support in either the repository or the post. The code is released under the MPL-2.0 licence.

CryptPad 2026.10.0

The autumn release that CryptPad, an end-to-end encrypted collaboration suite, previewed in its summer status report (covered in an earlier article) was published on GitHub on 21 October as 2026.10.0. According to the release notes, this version rewrites CryptPad's server, and the office document editors have moved from OnlyOffice to the compatible Euro Office. Self-hosting administrators should read the upgrade notes before upgrading, because the upgrade involves changes to the reverse proxy configuration and the configuration file is now split in two.

As of 23 October, the official blog had no announcement of this release. The summer status report mentioned that cryptpad.fr would drop French-language customer support, and as of the same day we still could not find a date for it.

PipePipe 5.5.0

PipePipe, the open-source YouTube client covered in an earlier article, released 5.5.0 on GitHub on 21 October. The release notes list multi-select on list pages, regular expression support in keyword filters, and filtering comments by keyword, username or like count. The third-party repository IzzyOnDroid updated to 5.5.0 the same day, while F-Droid's package page still showed 5.4.0 as of 23 October.

Civil rights suit against Florida state troopers

An earlier article covered a civil rights suit in the US District Court for the Middle District of Florida. The plaintiff had been arrested over a hit-and-run and was later not prosecuted, and the case involves license plate reader records. She sued two state troopers, and on 3 August the court stayed the case so that the parties could go to mediation.

The docket on CourtListener (a free database of US court dockets) lists a mediation report on 21 September and an order on 22 October. We could not find the contents of either entry in free public sources, and as of 23 October we had found no news reports of a mediation outcome or of the case resuming.

item.title: The per-app clipboard read toggle in GrapheneOS
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: GrapheneOS, a privacy-hardened mobile operating system officially supported only on Pixel phones, added Secure Paste in a release announced on 18 September, letting users set app by app which apps cannot read content copied in other apps. As of 23 October the feature is off by default and has to be turned on in settings, and the settings GrapheneOS adds are in English only. Stock Android notifies users after an app has read the clipboard, while iPhone asks for permission before an app reads it programmatically. Having a password manager clear the clipboard after copying a password is a step available on both.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 19 sources, including GrapheneOS, GrapheneOS Discussion Forum, GitHub

GrapheneOS is a privacy-hardened mobile operating system built on Android's open-source code, and as of 23 October its officially supported devices are the Pixel 6 through the Pixel 10a. Release 2026091700, announced on the official forum on 18 September, added a clipboard control called Secure Paste. According to the release notes, users can turn off clipboard reading app by app, or use a global toggle to make it off by default for all third-party apps. Users can still paste into those apps through the system selection toolbar, keyboard apps, keyboard shortcuts or accessibility services.

According to GrapheneOS's features page, Android only lets the focused app and the keyboard read the clipboard. Android shows a notice when an app reads content copied in another app, but by then the content has already been read. With Secure Paste on, an app cannot read content copied in other apps but can still read what it copied itself.

Secure Paste does not block reads by default: GrapheneOS described it as an opt-in feature in a reply on Mastodon, and the default in the settings code allows reads. According to the settings code, the toggle is at "Settings > Security & privacy > Privacy controls > Clipboard access", a path the official usage guide does not give. The global default can be "Allow" or "Blocked", and each app can be set to "Allow", "Paste only" or "Follow system clipboard access setting" to follow the global default, with a note in the settings code that Paste only may break some apps. Release 2026091900 then cut the interval between notices about blocked reads from 1 minute to 6 seconds (the notice can be turned off per app), release 2026092500 improved the settings screen, and the release notes list no further clipboard changes up to release 2026102100 on 21 October.

Per the descriptions in the settings code, the global toggle does not apply to system apps, and the current keyboard plus some apps and system features can always read the clipboard. Apps can still see whether the clipboard has content, its type and when it was copied, and accessibility services that can view and act on screen content can trigger a paste and may obtain what is pasted. According to the features page, with Paste only set, pasting into apps that draw their own selection toolbar (such as apps written with Flutter, a cross-platform development framework) means using the keyboard's paste button instead. GrapheneOS added that button to its default keyboard and Gboard already has one, according to replies on the official forum, so people using other keyboards should check that theirs can paste.

Perspective

According to Microsoft's security blog in 2023, mobile users often use the clipboard to copy sensitive content such as passwords and payment information. Android apps can read and write the clipboard without user consent or any specific permission.

In the same post Microsoft published its findings that an old version of a shopping app read the clipboard periodically and sent the content back to a server when it matched a certain format. The post adds that Microsoft was not aware of any specific malicious intent, and the behaviour was removed in May 2022. Since Android 10, background apps cannot read the clipboard, but that restriction does nothing about apps in the foreground.

According to the Android developer documentation, since Android 12 the system shows a notice the first time an app reads content copied in another app. Android 13 also shows a preview when content is copied, to confirm the copy worked. Apple's developer documentation states that since iOS 16 the system asks the user for permission before an app reads the clipboard programmatically. MacRumors reported in 2022 that from iOS 16.1, apps that have requested to paste get a "Paste from Other Apps" option in Settings, which we have not checked against the current iOS.

We suggest that GrapheneOS users first switch a few apps to Paste only, then decide whether to set the global default to Blocked, pasting through the toolbar or keyboard instead (after checking that their keyboard has a paste key). Both the warning in the settings code and the limitations GrapheneOS lists suggest that blocking everything at once is more likely to break some apps. If an app stops working properly after the change, it can be switched back to Allow.

According to GrapheneOS's features page, Secure Paste replaces the standard approach of desktop and mobile operating systems, and stock Android phones have no per-app toggle. On iPhone an app asks before reading programmatically, and on both platforms users can start by checking their password manager. 1Password's support page states that passwords copied from it are cleared automatically after 90 seconds by default on every platform. We suggest that people using other password managers look in the settings for an option to clear the clipboard, keeping in mind that timed clearing only shortens how long content stays on the clipboard, and the focused app can still read it before it is cleared.

Anyone who wants to install GrapheneOS first needs a supported Pixel, and according to the official FAQ GrapheneOS cannot be installed on carrier-locked devices, mainly those from US carriers. The official web installer page lists the requirements: the device running the installer needs at least 2GB of free memory and 32GB of free storage, and it can be a computer or an Android phone or tablet. By our inference from the settings code directory as checked on 23 October, the settings and apps GrapheneOS adds are in English only, while the rest of the system keeps Android's own translations, including Simplified and Traditional Chinese.

We, a community based in Taiwan, also checked the Google Store's list of regions in Asia for the supported phones. As of 23 October, Google Store Help lists the Asian places where the Pixel 10a, a GrapheneOS-supported model, can be bought as India, Japan, Singapore and Taiwan, while mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau and South Korea are not on the list. The page covers only the Google Store itself, not other retailers or carriers.

According to GrapheneOS's FAQ, its System Updater fetches update information and update files from releases.grapheneos.org. GreatFire, which measures censorship in mainland China, recorded interference with that address in its last test on 2 October, the only conclusive test in the 90 days before 23 October. By our inference, downloading system updates over a direct connection from mainland China may not go smoothly.

GrapheneOS users who switch apps to Paste only are blocking apps from reading on their own, but not accessibility services they have turned on or the keyboard they are using. The cost is that some apps need the keyboard's paste key instead.

item.title: Browser fingerprinting and how browsers defend against it
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: A browser fingerprint combines traits a website can read, such as window size, fonts and small differences in rendering, into an identifier that recognises the same browser again, and clearing cookies or using a VPN does not stop it. According to the UK Information Commissioner's Office, Google stopped prohibiting its advertising customers from using fingerprinting in February 2025. How much gets blocked depends on the browser, with Firefox, Safari, Brave and Tor Browser each taking their own approach. The only fingerprinting-related item on Chrome's official status page, as we checked it on 23 October, limits the data the browser attaches to every request automatically.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 25 sources, including Information Commissioner's Office, Google Marketing Platform Help, Google

In a personal blog post titled "Fingerprints are the new cookies", the author surveys the ways websites recognise a browser beyond cookies. According to a September 2025 document from the W3C Privacy Working Group, browser fingerprinting is a website's ability to recognise a visitor, browser or device from its configuration or other observable traits, such as window size, fonts and small differences in rendering. According to the UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) on 19 December 2024, Google stopped prohibiting organisations that use its advertising products from employing fingerprinting from 16 February 2025. How much gets blocked depends on the browser, with Firefox, Safari, Brave and Tor Browser each taking their own approach.

According to the same W3C document, clearing cookies or using a VPN does not prevent further correlation, and a fingerprint usually cannot be cleared or reset. In the document's assessment, technical measures already widely deployed are unlikely to remove fingerprinting entirely against a determined tracker, though specifications can still reduce it.

According to Google's 2019 blog post, users cannot clear a fingerprint and so cannot control how their information is collected, and Google at the time considered using fingerprints to track users wrong. In its December 2024 announcement to advertisers, Google tied the policy update to privacy-enhancing technologies and new ad channels such as connected TV, and neither that announcement nor the February 2025 policy update page mentions fingerprinting. "No longer prohibited" is the ICO's account of Google's notice to advertisers, a phrase that appears on neither of Google's public pages, and the ICO called the change irresponsible.

According to the ICO, under data protection rules such as the UK's Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR), companies must give users a fair choice before using fingerprinting and obtain consent where needed. These rules apply in the UK, and we, a community based in Taiwan, found no rule in Taiwan aimed specifically at device fingerprinting.

Google had planned to phase out third-party cookies in Chrome (small files that ad or analytics services embedded in web pages store in the browser to recognise users across sites), and on 22 July 2024 proposed letting users choose instead. On 22 April 2025 Google announced it would not roll out a separate prompt, leaving users to choose in Chrome's privacy and security settings. On 17 October 2025 Google announced it would retire most of Privacy Sandbox (a set of browser technologies Google proposed to replace third-party cookies), including IP Protection, which masks IP addresses. On the Privacy Sandbox status page as we checked it on 23 October (updated 14 August 2026), the only fingerprinting-related item limits the data the browser attaches to every request automatically, such as the browser version and operating system strings.

Perspective

In a 2024 WebKit post on Safari's Private Browsing, defences against fingerprinting fall into two kinds. One makes many users share the same fingerprint, the other shows each website a different one. Tor Browser takes the first approach, and according to its support page, making every user exactly identical is practically impossible, so the goal is to reduce the number of distinguishable groups for each trait.

Brave uses both. According to Brave's documentation, it makes Brave browsers look as alike as possible while adding a small amount of random noise. The seed for that noise differs for each session and each site, which makes it hard for sites to link the same person, and Brave's help centre lists blocking fingerprinting as on by default in Shields.

According to Mozilla's November 2025 announcement, the fingerprinting protections added in Firefox 145 are turned on first in Private Browsing and in Enhanced Tracking Protection's Strict mode, and at the time work was under way to make them the default. According to WebKit's September 2025 post on Safari 26.0, Safari prevents known fingerprinting scripts from reliably reading information that can reveal device traits, such as screen dimensions and audio.

Safari also has an advanced fingerprinting protection that can apply to Private Browsing only or to all browsing. Apple's June 2025 iOS 26 press release describes this protection as extending to all browsing by default, while Apple's Safari help page gives no default, so we suggest checking the setting yourself. According to the 2024 WebKit post, on iPhone it is under "Settings > Apps > Safari > Advanced > Advanced Tracking and Fingerprinting Protection", where you choose "All Browsing". On a Mac it is in Safari's Advanced settings, where you turn on "Use advanced tracking and fingerprinting protection" and apply it to all browsing.

Readers using Firefox on desktop can get the protections added in version 145 by switching Enhanced Tracking Protection from Standard to Strict under Privacy & Security. We could not find the default on mobile.

People who need stronger protection and can accept slower connections can switch to Tor Browser, which the EFF page we checked on 23 October also lists as the most practical option. The Tor Project's page on fingerprinting protections is available in Traditional and Simplified Chinese. According to our docs site, Android has an official Tor Browser and iPhone does not.

To see how easily your own browser can be recognised, you can open the EFF's Cover Your Tracks, whose pages we found are all in English. According to the site, it collects only anonymous data and compares you with visitors who tested recently, and how each browser's defences differ is also covered on our docs site in A browser fingerprint cannot be cleared the way a cookie can.

Stronger protection makes websites more likely to break. According to Mozilla's announcement, more aggressive blocking will inevitably break legitimate site features, for example calendar and meeting tools that need the real time zone. According to the Tor support page, inconsistent traits can lead anti-bot systems to treat Tor users as bots, and the EFF page includes a caution that a protection can itself sometimes become part of the fingerprint.

None of the official pages and statutes we read in Japan, South Korea or mainland China mentions browser fingerprinting by name as of 23 October, but each addresses the data behind tracking differently. Japan amended its Telecommunications Business Act in June 2022, in force since 16 June 2023, so that services such as messaging, social media, search and news sites sending users' devices a program that transmits user data to outside parties must give notice of what is sent, publish it, obtain consent or offer an opt-out. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications page, information truly necessary to provide the service, such as OS, screen and language settings and browser information, is exempt from the notice-or-publication requirement, as is an ID the service itself stored in a first-party cookie.

South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission draws the line at identification in a policy plan published on 31 January 2024, a set of recommendations rather than a statute. Under the plan, ad companies may process online behavioural data without consent if they do not identify a specific person, but must keep the data from becoming identifying through accumulation, overlap or combination, and need consent when they do identify someone. According to the plan, revised guidelines were due by the end of 2024, and as of 18 October we could not find whether they were issued or are in force.

Mainland China's Personal Information Protection Law sets its rule at automated decision-making instead. Article 24 requires that information push and commercial marketing based on automated decision-making also offer an option not targeted at personal characteristics, or a convenient way to refuse. The Cyberspace Administration of China's January Q&A on personal information lists user identifiers, browsing records, device information such as the IMEI, and user profiles as personal information.

Our reading is that these settings reduce a website's ability to recognise the same person when the reader is not logged in, while Brave's approach is aimed specifically at linking across sites and sessions. A website where you are logged in to the same account still knows who is browsing.

item.title: A static website hosted as a Tor onion service
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Hosting an onion service needs no fixed IP address, domain name or open port, and tor plus an ordinary web server is enough to put a static site on the Tor network. tor shipped four security updates between June and October, three with fixes involving onion services, and as of 20 October the latest is 0.4.9.14. Visitors need to connect through Tor, for example with Tor Browser.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including Tor Project, Riseup, Personal blog

In June, an author described on a personal blog how they put their static website on a Tor onion service (a site reachable only through Tor, with the server's location protected), using tor, the Tor Project's core program, and the nginx web server. According to the Tor Project's page on onion service properties, an onion service needs no fixed IP address, no domain name and no open port. Between 25 June and 7 October, tor shipped four security releases, 0.4.9.11 to 0.4.9.14, three of them with fixes involving onion services, and as of 20 October the latest is 0.4.9.14.

Anyone already running an onion service should update to the latest version. Visitors to such a site need to connect through Tor, for example with Tor Browser.

Following the post and the official setup guide, the operator names a directory for the keys and a local port to forward to in tor's configuration file, torrc. After tor restarts, the hostname file in that directory holds the site's .onion address. The web server listens only on the local machine, and according to the post Tor already encrypts the connection, so no separate TLS (the encryption behind HTTPS) is needed. Static site generators write the site's address into internal links, so the author builds a second copy based on the .onion address, which keeps visitors on the onion service from being sent back to the ordinary address.

The setup guide's further advice is to forward to a Unix socket (a channel that programs on the same computer use to exchange data) instead of a local network port, so the service does not leak onto the local network. The guide also warns that an onion service set up this way can be read by anyone who knows the address. To limit it to particular people, client authorization lets only those holding a private key connect. According to the Onion-Location page, operators of an existing HTTPS site can add that header so Tor Browser shows the .onion version in the address bar when someone opens the original site.

Perspective

According to the official overview, an onion service's name is the public key used to authenticate the connection, so no certificate authority (the bodies that issue HTTPS certificates to websites) is needed. Tor encrypts the connection all the way from the user to the service. The service only makes outbound connections and can get through NAT (the mechanism home and organisational networks use to share one public IP address), so it can run on school or office networks where ports cannot be opened. According to the properties page, an onion service is reachable whenever the user can reach the Tor network and the service is online, regardless of DNS and IP blocking.

According to the official Operational Security page, whether the server's location stays hidden depends on how the operator maintains the system. A web server may reveal its software and operating system, and a computer that is not always online also leaks information. The longer a service runs, the higher the risk that its location is found. The same page recommends adding Vanguards (an add-on that reduces the risk of a service's entry relays being traced) to guard against advanced attacks.

The setup guide calls keeping a server from revealing its location "not an easy task" and lists the Operational Security page and Riseup's guide for reference. Riseup's guide recommends NTP (network time synchronisation) to keep the server clock correct, so clock drift cannot be used to identify the server. For people who have never run a web server, the setup guide suggests trying OnionShare, which has a graphical interface and fewer settings. The Tor Project's Onionspray adds an onion entrance to an existing public website, and its documentation lists that it is not suited to onion-only sites and does not protect the site's location.

The documentation for Arti, the Tor implementation rewritten in the Rust programming language, is inconsistent on whether it can host onion services. As of 20 October, Arti's project page says this is implemented, while its capability and limitations page says it is only partly done and off by default. The Onionspray documentation also says it relies on the C implementation of tor until Arti offers an alternative. Our inference from these documents is that tor is the safer choice for a production deployment.

Readers whose access to ordinary websites is blocked but who can still reach Tor can also read sites hosted as onion services. Our inference from the Operational Security page is that hosting one needs a machine that can stay on for long periods. The official examples mainly use Debian, the process is editing a configuration file on the command line with no programming required, and the guide has a Traditional Chinese translation (as of 20 October some sections are still in English).

Tor Metrics and OONI publish figures for mainland China, Taiwan and Hong Kong. Tor Metrics estimates, as daily averages for 11 to 17 October, about 1,055 users connecting directly from mainland China, against about 9,518 from Taiwan and about 8,253 from Hong Kong. These are estimates of direct connections only and leave out users who connect through bridges.

OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference) Tor tests from 18 September to 18 October numbered 301 in mainland China, 293 of them flagged as anomalies and none confirmed as blocked. Hong Kong had 706 tests with 7 anomalies, and Taiwan 4,797 tests with 314 anomalies, 311 of them from a single ASN (autonomous system number, which identifies one network). An anomaly is not a confirmed block, and the test checks whether the servers Tor needs to operate are reachable, not onion services themselves.

For mainland China, the Tor Project's support page advises letting Tor Browser's Connection Assist try bridges or Snowflake automatically first, then WebTunnel bridges, then Snowflake and meek (meek has limited bandwidth and is slower). That page covers reaching the Tor network and does not say whether onion services are reachable from mainland China. As of 20 October we found no rules specifically on running onion services in mainland China, Taiwan or Hong Kong.

According to the properties page, a site can still record data about users once they log in. Our inference from the Operational Security page is that what the site's own content reveals is up to the operator.

item.title: AISeal, the isolated environment for on-device AI in Android 17
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 7 October Google described AISeal in Android 17, which keeps the personal data used by on-device AI in a protected virtual machine isolated from the operating system. According to the announcement, the first phase covers storing personal data, with model inference and AI agents to follow. As of 20 October, Google had not said which devices or regions have it enabled, and there is nothing in Google's announcement or help pages about settings that users need to change.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 13 sources, including Google, Android Open Source Project, Android Developers

On 7 October, Google described on its official blog how AISeal (Android on-device AI seal) in Android 17 puts the personal data that on-device AI uses into a protected virtual machine isolated from the Android operating system. According to the announcement, it is designed so that personal data stays cryptographically isolated even if the whole operating system is compromised. The first phase covers only storing personal data, with model inference and AI agents (AI that carries out multi-step tasks on the user's behalf) to come later. As of 20 October, Google had not said which devices or regions have it enabled, and there is nothing in Google's announcement or help pages about settings that users need to change.

According to the announcement, AISeal is built on the Android Virtualization Framework (AVF) and pKVM, a hypervisor (the low-level software that partitions and isolates virtual machines). The protected space is designed to hold three kinds of services at once: an encrypted personal database, model inference running on the device, and AI agents that combine the two. In the announcement's example, an assistant queries the personal database and summarizes your schedule inside the isolated space, and outbound controls are designed to let only the final answer return to the operating system (something only possible once inference moves into AISeal). According to the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) documentation, even if the host (the Android system that normally runs apps) is compromised, it cannot read the protected virtual machine's memory.

On the chip side, according to the announcement, MediaTek has announced support on the Dimensity 9600 Pro, and Qualcomm's Snapdragon chipsets will support AISeal through AVF. pKVM itself received SESIP (a security evaluation scheme) Level 5 certification in 2025, described in the announcement as the highest vulnerability testing tier under ISO 15408 (the announcement does not say AISeal itself is certified). According to the source code tagged Android 17, AOSP already includes the AISeal framework. In the same source code, the service is off by default and only starts once the device property service.aiseal.enable is set to 1, a step that by our inference the phone maker takes.

Perspective

Android's existing isolation consists of the app sandbox, SELinux policies and Private Compute Core. According to the Private Compute Services documentation, features inside Private Compute Core cannot connect to the network directly and reach it only through a set of open-source APIs. What AISeal adds is a layer of memory isolation carved out by the hypervisor. According to the AVF security documentation, the part of pKVM that runs at the hypervisor level is roughly 10,000 lines of code, against roughly 20 million for the whole Linux kernel (an attack surface three orders of magnitude smaller).

According to the same security documentation, companies that handle the supply chain, such as phone makers and chip vendors, still have to be trusted, and the host can affect whether a virtual machine runs normally. Encrypted storage, per the same document, has no rollback protection at the block level (there is no way to detect encrypted data being swapped back to an older version). These are design limits of pKVM and protected virtual machines, and by our inference they apply equally to AISeal, which is built on top of them.

According to a technical blog post analysing the Android 17 source code, the host can still see data at the moment it is collected, before it is stored in AISeal. By the same analysis, AISeal does not separate the data from the AI service provider the user chooses.

In the source code tagged Android 17, AISeal's management interface requires the signature|privileged permission, which by our inference ordinary third-party apps cannot obtain. Gemini Nano, Google's on-device model available to developers, runs in AICore, the system service that manages on-device models, and integrating AICore with AISeal is listed in the announcement as a future plan. Digital Trends cautioned that chip support for AISeal does not mean the assistant on a phone actually runs inside AISeal, since that depends on how the phone maker implements it.

According to Google's help pages, as of 20 October both the Gemini web app and the Gemini mobile apps are available in Hong Kong, Japan, Macau, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan. Mainland China is missing from the mobile app list and limited to Workspace accounts on the web.

We found no list of the devices, countries or languages where AISeal is enabled in Google's announcement, the AOSP documentation or news coverage, so Gemini's availability in a place is no indication of AISeal there. Other features' regional lists are no guide either. According to its help page, Magic Cue, Pixel's personal suggestions feature, lists Japan but not Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea or mainland China, and nothing on that page says Magic Cue uses AISeal.

Readers do not need to change any settings now, and as of 20 October there is no user-facing switch in Google's announcement or help pages. What is worth watching is when Google or phone makers publish the devices and regions where AISeal is enabled, and when model inference and AI agents move into it.

Following Digital Trends' caveat, our inference is that when buying a phone you can check whether the maker's specifications and help pages state that AI features run inside AISeal. Per the technical blog analysis cited above, even with features running inside AISeal, data at the moment of collection and the AI service provider the user chooses remain outside the isolation.

item.title: Coordinated disclosure of the PHP vulnerabilities and publication before the fix
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: News of two PHP vulnerabilities leaked during coordinated disclosure. Before the fix came out on 21 October, a researcher published what were claimed to be full technical details, and a distributor released images containing the fix early. Security firms also deployed protections for their customers ahead of time. This piece sets out the different views on embargoes and early publication, the relevant guidance and rules in the US, the EU and mainland China, and how Japan and Taiwan handle disclosure timing.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including The PHP Foundation, The Register, The Record

News of two vulnerabilities that PHP fixed on 21 October (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), which may let an attacker who is not logged in run code on a web server, leaked while coordinated disclosure was under way. Before the fix was released, a researcher published what were claimed to be full technical details, and some companies shipped the fix early or deployed protections for their customers. Security practitioners have since been debating whether anyone can or should publish before a fix is released, or protect some people first. Organisations whose websites run on PHP should first confirm with their host or contractor that the fix has been applied, as our previous article describes, while this debate bears on when future vulnerabilities become known and who hears about them first.

In coordinated vulnerability disclosure, whoever finds a vulnerability tells the developers privately first, and they agree on a date for publication. The period of secrecy before that date is called an embargo, and it gives the developers and downstream distributors (companies that package software such as PHP for users to install) time to prepare a fix.

According to a PHP Foundation blog post on 21 October, the coordinated disclosure worked well until two days before the planned release date. At around 15:00 UTC on 20 October (around 23:00 Taipei time), the vulnerability IDs began circulating online. At 19:30 UTC (03:30 on 21 October, Taipei time) PHP issued an announcement moving the release forward by a day, to 21 October.

The same post says that after the announcement, one of the security firms that had reported the vulnerabilities mistakenly published a demonstration video. Mitigation advice that PHP had given a small number of critical infrastructure providers from around 23:00 UTC on 20 October (07:00 on 21 October, Taipei time) may also have leaked. Chainguard, a distributor that had received the fix in advance like the other distributors, published container images (pre-packaged software environments ready to deploy) containing the fix at 07:41 UTC on 21 October (15:41 Taipei time). That was more than six hours before the brought-forward release, and in the post's words, "Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release."

According to an iTnews report on 21 October, a few hours after the vulnerability IDs appeared on social media, a researcher published what were claimed to be the full technical details online. iTnews had not independently confirmed that the material was valid. Security firm watchTowr's page says customers of its platform had active defences in place 24 hours before PHP released the fix. Cloudflare's blog post says its matching firewall rules went live about 9 hours before public disclosure and are enabled by default for free and paid customers.

Amazon's threat intelligence post of 21 October says its honeypot (a system deliberately placed on the internet to observe attacks) recorded exploitation attempts as early as 17 October, before the vulnerability IDs leaked. The post also says it is unclear whether these attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems, and how the attacker obtained the information before disclosure.

Perspective

Under the disclosure policy of CERT/CC, the US vulnerability coordination centre, vulnerabilities are published 45 days after the initial report, possibly earlier or later in circumstances such as active exploitation. CERT/CC's guide to coordinated disclosure notes that the more parties are involved and the longer an embargo lasts, the more likely a leak becomes.

The distros mailing list shared among distributions sets a maximum embargo of 14 days and prefers less than 7. Members may not share the information with anyone outside their team, nor deploy undocumented fixes for customers in advance. As of 22 October, we could not find out whether PHP notified distributions through distros.

Whether to publish early once a leak has happened is the first point of contention, and Chainguard's chief executive told The Register the company did not leak anything. He said people were already being attacked before the official disclosure, so the company decided to ship the fix first. In his words, "It's coordinated vulnerability disclosure, unless there's evidence of active exploits in the wild." As of 22 October, we had not found a written statement published by Chainguard itself.

The multi-party coordination guidelines of FIRST, the international body of incident response teams, limit a reasonable embargo to cases where there is no clear evidence of prior public disclosure, including active exploitation. Before the fix was released, Amazon's honeypot recorded exploitation attempts, though it was uncertain whether they would succeed against real systems. Cloudflare's blog post also says attack traffic aimed at its customers was observed during the leak.

According to the PHP Foundation's post, Chainguard broke the embargo unilaterally, disregarding weeks of coordination by many parties. According to The Register, Chainguard's chief executive had notified PHP's coordinated disclosure channel in advance. On Hacker News, some commenters argued that if breaking an embargo has no consequences it will keep happening, and others that this case had already damaged the trust coordinated disclosure depends on. The PHP Foundation's post also says that by the time of public release, the PHP security team had not found a working exploit among the proofs of concept in circulation.

Who gets protected early is the second point of contention, and Hacker News comments defending early publication argued that coordinated disclosure left ordinary users unable to protect themselves. Customers of watchTowr's platform were protected 24 hours before PHP released the fix, while Cloudflare's protective rules were enabled by default for both free and paid customers. According to The Register, Chainguard's images were available to anyone.

PHP's post says that distributions and long-term support vendors received the fix in advance, while the mitigation advice went to a small number of critical infrastructure providers. The post explains that PHP did not release immediately after the leak because distributions were still packaging the fix, and releasing at once would have left many users without an easy way to update. As of 22 October, we had found no public criticism of who was on the advance notification list.

Chainguard's chief executive also told The Register that just being told a piece of software has a vulnerability is enough to find it, which he sees as the new normal. Amazon's post likewise holds that an embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug, while maintaining that coordinated disclosure is still the right model. It reminds defenders not to assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation, since AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch or advisory into a working exploit.

Whether publishing vulnerability details before a fix is illegal depends on where it happens. The digital rights group EFF, in an FAQ written for US researchers, takes the position that the law should only rarely police disclosures, and that disclosure outside the "responsible disclosure" model may also be legal. The FAQ notes that it is not legal advice. It also says that the more functional code a disclosure contains, the riskier it is.

Mainland China's Regulations on the Management of Network Product Security Vulnerabilities, in force since September 2021, apply to network product providers within the People's Republic of China and to organisations or individuals who discover, collect or publish vulnerabilities. The text does not say whether "within" also limits the latter group. The regulations prohibit publishing vulnerability information before the product provider offers a fix, and anyone who thinks early publication is necessary must consult the provider and report to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the Ministry of Public Security, which assess the case before publication. They also prohibit publishing programs and tools designed specifically to exploit vulnerabilities for activities that endanger network security.

Article 7 of the EU Directive on attacks against information systems (Directive 2013/40/EU) requires member states to punish, at least in cases that are not minor, the production or making available without right of programs designed primarily to commit offences, with the intention that they be used for such offences. As of 22 October, we could not find how member states have transposed it into national law, or any EU guidance on publishing vulnerability information as such. Comparing the EFF's summary with the EU directive, we found that both look at intent and content. Mainland China's regulations look at content too, but also restrict the timing of publication directly.

We, a community based in Taiwan, also compared how Japan and Taiwan set the timing of disclosure, using the rules as we checked them on 8 October, without assessing how either would apply to this incident. Japan's Information Security Early Warning Partnership has operated since July 2004 under public notices of the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, with the Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA) receiving reports and JPCERT/CC (Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center) contacting developers and coordinating when information is published. Its guidelines, in a 2026 edition published on 1 October, set a target of 45 days after JPCERT/CC first tries to reach the developer, taking into account the time a fix needs, coordination with counterparts abroad, the risk of the information leaking and the risk of exploitation.

The Japanese guidelines also cover who hears first. A developer may warn its users before the publication date, after coordinating with JPCERT/CC, where it judges this would reduce user risk, and for open source software JPCERT/CC notifies the developers or development community and, where necessary, distributors and the developers of products that include it. Under the 2026 edition, IPA also promptly notifies the Cabinet Office of vulnerabilities that are exploited or suspected of being exploited, or that are severe and would have a wide impact if exploited, and the Cabinet Office may pass information to developers, government bodies, infrastructure operators and users before IPA and JPCERT/CC publish, in parallel with the usual process, under which JPCERT/CC's coordination and publication normally proceed as before.

In Taiwan, the vulnerability disclosure policy of TWCERT/CC (Taiwan Computer Emergency Response Team/Coordination Center), version 2.2 dated 18 March 2025, says it publishes a report's basic details within 90 calendar days of confirming that the report is complete, and may delay publication or limit the detail after assessing the impact. The full details go on its Taiwan Vulnerability Note (TVN) platform only after the reporter, TWCERT/CC and the vendor all confirm that a fix or mitigation is in place. The policy defines a vendor as the manufacturer of the affected product and does not mention open source projects or development communities, and does not say whether it applies to ones based abroad.

In Japan, IPA does not require reporters to keep information secret or developers to fix the flaw, and the guidelines contain no penalty provisions, though they note that IPA accepting a report does not relieve the reporter of legal liability for how the vulnerability was found. Taiwan's policy says it follows the CVE program's rules (the system that assigns vulnerability IDs) and the laws of the Republic of China without citing a specific statute, and we did not check reporting obligations under Taiwan's Cyber Security Management Act or other laws. In our reading, the documents in both places set the timing that the coordinating body itself works to, which puts them closer to the CERT/CC policy and the distros list than to mainland China's regulations, where publication before a fix is generally prohibited and violations are referred to MIIT and the Ministry of Public Security, with penalties under Article 62 of the PRC Cybersecurity Law where it applies. The regulations themselves set no fine, and we did not check that article.

Our advice is that organisations whose websites run on PHP ask their host or contractor to confirm that the fix has been applied, and check their logs. Amazon recommends checking logs from at least 17 October, because it recorded exploitation attempts that day. Amazon also recommends measuring patch and mitigation timelines in hours for critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, saying a 7-day or 30-day deadline is no longer enough. For the questions to ask your host or contractor, and the checks to run after patching, see Checking and responding to a critical vulnerability on your organisation's website on the docs site.

The PHP Foundation's post says the foundation is changing the security team's decision-making so that vulnerabilities stuck on hard trade-offs reach its leadership sooner. Chainguard's chief executive told The Record that the industry has to figure out how to get through such situations "faster and more coordinated and better." As of 22 October, the post did not mention changing the length of embargoes, the advance notification list or how those who break an embargo are handled. FIRST's guidelines suggest that sharing communities could set penalties for members who violate trust, such as removal from the community.

Readers comparing these approaches can ask a few questions. Whom does an embargo protect, how is the list of those who get early notice and protection decided, and do ordinary users have any way to protect themselves during the embargo? When a fix ships early, are the majority who are still waiting exposed to attackers first? And if, as Amazon says, AI-assisted analysis speeds up building exploits, how much time can an embargo still buy?
