item.title: PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities and the early leak of their IDs
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 21 October PHP released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, fixing two vulnerabilities that may let an attacker who is not logged in run code on a web server. The vulnerability IDs leaked two days before the planned disclosure, and PHP moved the release forward by a day. The flaws are in PHP itself, so the PHP on the server is what needs updating, and people on hosted plans can check with their provider.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 25 sources, including PHP, The PHP Foundation, WordPress.org

PHP released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 on 21 October, fixing two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which researchers and the media call php2shell. The php.net advisory says both may allow an attacker who is not logged in to execute code remotely on the server, that every PHP installation handling web requests is at risk, and that users should update immediately. According to W3Techs statistics for 21 October, 69.3% of websites whose server-side language is known use PHP. WordPress.org's announcement explains that this is not a vulnerability in WordPress itself and that no WordPress update will be released for it, since the PHP on the server is what needs updating.

According to a PHP Foundation blog post on 21 October, the two CVE IDs began circulating on forums and social media at around 15:00 UTC on 20 October (23:00 Taipei time). They came with a wrong release time and a wrong severity score (CVSS, out of 10) of 10.0, where PHP's own rating is 9.2, and no technical details leaked. At 19:30 UTC (03:30 on 21 October, Taipei time) PHP brought its pre-announcement forward and moved the release from 14:00 UTC on 22 October to 14:00 UTC on 21 October (22:00 Taipei time). It did not release at once because Linux distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu and Red Hat were still packaging the fix, and releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update.

The same post says that after the pre-announcement, one of the security firms that had reported the vulnerabilities mistakenly published a demonstration video, and copies quickly spread on social media. In the post's account, the video was one of the reasons various parties sped up work on proofs of concept (PoCs, code showing that a vulnerability can be exploited). By the time of public release, the PHP security team had not found a working exploit among the PoCs in circulation.

Cloudflare's blog post of 21 October says it observed attack traffic aimed at its customers during the leak, and that matching WAF (web application firewall) rules have been enabled by default for free and paid customers since 03:02 UTC on 21 October (11:02 Taipei time). As of 16:30 US Eastern Time on 21 October (04:30 on 22 October, Taipei time), security firm Huntress had not observed exploitation on its partners' systems. After the fixed versions came out, Taiwan's TWCERT/CC (Taiwan Computer Emergency Response Team/Coordination Center) noted in an alert on 22 October that PoCs had appeared online.

Perspective

According to the PHP Foundation's post, both vulnerabilities sit in memory management and error handling, parts of PHP that nearly every request touches. The php.net advisory describes the first as occurring when memory use reaches its limit, at which point PHP may be interrupted while internal data is only partly initialised. A later clean-up step may then treat that data as valid.

The second involves internal state left behind by an earlier request, which may be used by a later request handled by the same worker process after its memory has been freed. The php.net advisory rates Apache with mod_php (a setup that loads PHP directly into the web server) as the highest risk, and an exploit has been demonstrated in which an unauthenticated request triggers the attack before the site's own code runs.

According to php2shell.com, an explainer site set up by the researchers, the flaws are in PHP itself, so even a securely written site can be affected, including a simple one that only prints "Hello World". Automattic, the company that runs WordPress.com, likewise explains that this is a fix to the runtime, and that updating WordPress, themes or plugins alone does not protect against it.

The PHP Foundation's post also looks at why the fix took so long. During an external security audit in 2024, PHP developers had already found early signs of the first vulnerability, though no path to remote code execution was known at the time. Each of the fixes considered then had a cost, whether breaking compatibility, opening up denial of service (making a site stop working normally) or requiring changes to many third-party extensions. The security team, which operates by consensus, struggled to choose, and the post calls the delay "a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources."

The same post says AI-assisted vulnerability research has brought PHP far more reports than before. Since 1 July the security team has published 15 CVEs and handled more than 100 reports that were invalid, duplicates or could not be reproduced. The PHP Foundation is changing its process so that serious vulnerabilities stuck on hard trade-offs reach its leadership sooner.

Japan's Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA) announced on 21 October when the fix would be published. That evening, according to ITmedia NEWS, Japan's prime minister urged organisations on X to prepare to apply it, adding that temporarily taking a website offline is one effective way to reduce the risk where patching is difficult.

According to a tally by the security blog piyolog, compiled from organisations' notices and news reports, 211 organisations in Japan had suspended services or announced emergency maintenance by just after 1 a.m. Japan time on 22 October (just after midnight Taipei time), including 2 national government bodies and 4 local governments. Sapporo took its official website offline on the evening of 21 October. As of 22 October, its temporary home page said no unauthorised access or tampering had been found and that the shutdown was a precaution.

On 22 October the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) published guidance for companies, recommending that those unable to update or to apply interim settings consider blocking external access or temporarily suspending services. It also asks companies to check logs from at least 20 October onwards after updating, and recommends changing database passwords, API keys and administrator passwords on servers that were exposed to the internet before the update.

Taiwan's Administration for Cyber Security, under the Ministry of Digital Affairs, issued a press release the same day asking organisations to take stock of their PHP systems and patch them, without asking anyone to suspend services. As of 22 October we, a community based in Taiwan, found no notices of Taiwanese organisations going offline over these flaws, and no confirmed intrusions in Japan, South Korea or Taiwan.

We also compared the rules on disclosure timing in mainland China, Japan and Taiwan as of 8 October. What follows summarises each system, and we have not assessed how any of them would apply to this incident.

In mainland China, the Regulations on the Management of Network Product Security Vulnerabilities, in force since September 2021, apply to network product providers and operators in mainland China and to those who discover, collect or publish vulnerabilities. They require providers to report a vulnerability to a platform run by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) within two days of discovering or learning of it. Anyone publishing vulnerability information may not do so before the provider offers a fix, and those who think early publication is necessary must consult the provider and report to MIIT and the Ministry of Public Security, which assess the case and publish. The regulations do not define whether open source maintainers count as providers, and we could not find whether they apply to maintainers of projects abroad or to researchers outside mainland China.

Under the 2026 edition of the guidelines for Japan's Information Security Early Warning Partnership, published on 1 October, IPA receives reports, and JPCERT/CC, the designated coordination body, contacts developers and arranges when information is published. The target, which is not a legal deadline, is 45 days after JPCERT/CC first tries to reach the developer, taking into account the time a fix needs, coordination with counterparts abroad, the risk of the information leaking and the risk of exploitation. For open source software, JPCERT/CC also notifies distributors and the developers of products that include it when necessary. IPA does not require reporters to keep the information secret, nor does it require developers to fix the flaw.

In Taiwan, TWCERT/CC's vulnerability disclosure policy (version 2.2, March 2025) says it publishes a report's basic details within 90 calendar days of confirming that the report is complete, though it may delay publication after assessing the impact. The full details go on its Taiwan Vulnerability Note (TVN) platform only after the reporter, TWCERT/CC and the vendor all confirm that a fix or mitigation is in place. The policy does not say whether it covers open source projects based abroad, and we did not check reporting obligations under Taiwan's laws such as the Cyber Security Management Act.

Organisations often build their websites and blogs on PHP software such as WordPress. According to Automattic, sites on its own managed services such as WordPress.com are already protected, and their administrators do not need to change any settings. WordPress.org's announcement advises people on hosted plans to check with their host about the update, and notes that the PHP version is shown in the dashboard under "Tools > Site Health > Info > Server" (in the English interface). That version number can be compared with the fixed versions above, but it can mislead when a distribution backports the fix, as the next paragraph explains.

People who run their own servers and installed PHP from distribution packages should check their distribution's security advisories. Some distributions backport the fix to the original version, so comparing only the PHP version number can mislead; Ubuntu 24.04's fixed package, for example, is 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.13. Red Hat's advisory of 21 October says Red Hat Enterprise Linux uses PHP-FPM (which runs PHP in separate processes) by default, making exploitation harder, and that some updates were still being prepared. The PHP Foundation's post, for its part, says the first vulnerability has also been confirmed to allow remote code execution on PHP-FPM through the site's own request handling.

According to php.net's supported versions page, PHP 8.1 and earlier have reached end of life, and 8.2 reaches end of life on 31 December 2026. For this release PHP also provided minimal source patches for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 for people who compile PHP themselves, but none for 7.3 or earlier. TWCERT/CC's alert lists affected versions from 5.4 onwards. For those who cannot update yet, php.net lists several configuration changes that narrow some attack paths, while warning that only updating fully resolves the problem.

Whether either vulnerability turns out to have been used in confirmed intrusions, whether they are added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog of the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and whether Red Hat and other distributions complete their updates are the things to watch next.

item.title: Weak private keys in eight eMudhra intermediate certificates
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Eight intermediate certificates from the Indian certificate authority eMudhra had private keys smaller than 256, which anyone could compute at once and use to issue HTTPS certificates for other people's websites. After a researcher reported it on 17 October, Chrome and Firefox blocked them automatically within hours, with nothing for ordinary browser users to set up. Programs that do not go through a browser carry their own trust lists, and Node.js, Python's certifi, Go, Java and Linux distributions have been shipping updates since 19 October (not all complete as of 22 October), so people who write their own code or run servers need to update each one.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 14 sources, including Mozilla dev-security-policy, Mozilla Bugzilla, Google

The Indian certificate authority eMudhra (certificate brand emSign) had eight intermediate certificates whose private keys were simple enough to calculate directly. Intermediate certificates sit below the root and are the layer actually used to sign website certificates. A researcher reported the problem to Apple, Chrome, Microsoft, Mozilla and eMudhra at 18:05 UTC on 17 October (02:05 on 18 October Taipei time), attaching proofs signed with each of the eight keys. According to Mozilla's 20 October post on the dev-security-policy mailing list, anyone holding the keys could issue HTTPS certificates for websites they do not own.

Chrome and Firefox blocked the six TLS intermediates within hours of the report through automatically pushed blocklists, so most users did not need to update or restart their browsers. The bigger exposure is in programs that do not go through a browser, such as tools and servers written in Node.js, Python, Go or Java, which each keep trusting the certificates until they are updated. Mozilla added on the incident ticket on 20 October that several people had independently computed the keys, and that some of them had made this public.

According to the preliminary analysis by Mozilla engineers on the Bugzilla incident ticket, all eight are P-384 elliptic-curve keys, each of which should be a randomly chosen 384-bit integer. The actual values were all below 256, so trying 256 numbers in turn is enough to find them. Six of the eight sign TLS certificates for websites and are trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, Microsoft and Apple, while the other two sign code and are trusted by Microsoft.

eMudhra's statement says the eight intermediates were created at a key generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, and the problem went unnoticed for about 18 months and through two independent audits. In eMudhra's preliminary explanation on the incident ticket, the software used in the ceremony was flawed and generated a set of weak keys alongside the intended ones. The two sets had similar labels, and the weak keys were mistakenly used to request the certificates. eMudhra's statement, updated on 21 October, also says the exact root cause is still under investigation.

According to the same statement, seven of the eight were never used in production, and the one in use had issued no certificates. eMudhra also says it knows of no evidence that anyone computed the weak keys before disclosure. Google's 20 October blog post says that before the block, Certificate Transparency (CT, the public logs that record every certificate) held no website certificates signed by the six intermediates. Because Chrome by default accepts only certificates logged in CT, Google concluded that forged certificates could not fool Chrome, nor Android apps that target the latest SDK or have opted in to CT checks.

An explainer page that a Mozilla engineer set up for the incident adds that many programs outside the browser do not check CT. The page also says the keys could have been abused ever since the certificates were created in April 2025, and that it is not known whether attackers used the weak keys against such programs.

Perspective

A browser trusts an HTTPS site because the site's certificate is signed layer by layer by a chain of certificate authorities, with the root certificate at the top preinstalled in the trust list of the browser or operating system. The private key of an intermediate certificate can sign a certificate for any domain. FreeBSD's 21 October security advisory says an attacker able to intercept network traffic could use the computed keys to impersonate any TLS server and read or modify the connection without being detected.

Chrome's CRLSet and Firefox's OneCRL are blocklists that the browsers download automatically in the background, and they can block a specific intermediate certificate on its own. Together with the CT requirement, Chrome and Firefox had two layers of protection on the day of the report. According to Mozilla's release notes and the incident ticket, Firefox installations with automatic list downloads (Remote Settings) disabled need to update to 158.0.1. Some Firefox for Android profiles did not apply the list at startup and need 158.0.2.

According to the Bugzilla incident ticket, eMudhra marked the eight intermediates as revoked on 18 October UTC. Mozilla wrote on the ticket that some programs do not read revocation information, or have no mechanism for distrusting a particular intermediate on its own. NSS is the cryptographic library maintained by Mozilla, and many programs and distributions reuse its root certificate list. To protect those programs, Mozilla removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3, the root that the six TLS intermediates chain up to, in NSS 3.131.1 on 20 October.

Node.js shipped the new list in 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 on 21 October, and Go released 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. The explainer page's list of fixes shows that Python's certifi 2026.10.19 and curl's CA bundle have been updated as well. Ubuntu's tracking bug shows ca-certificates updates released for 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 and 26.10 as of 22 October, with nothing yet for 20.04 and earlier. Fedora has submitted updates, but according to the Red Hat Bugzilla bug, as of 22 October they still trust the root that issued the two code-signing intermediates.

The explainer page advises ordinary users to update their browsers and operating systems to the latest version as soon as possible. According to Google's blog, Android devices received the same block through Google Play services around 22:00 UTC on 19 October (06:00 on 20 October Taipei time). Google says most Android devices have already received it, and those that have not can apply it immediately by restarting. Android devices without Google Play services fall outside what Google describes there, and we found no update to the Android system itself.

When we checked on 18 October, the third-party monitor GreatFire's last test (on 11 October) found play.google.com fully blocked in mainland China, with interference recorded since 10 March 2012. GreatFire measures whether websites can be reached, not whether Google Play services on a device can receive updates. We, a community based in Taiwan, infer from Google's description that Android devices without Google Play services, or whose Google Play services cannot connect, are not covered by the block it describes, while the CRLSet and OneCRL lists that browsers download themselves do not go through Google Play services. The explanation page's advice to ordinary users is to update the browser and system to the latest version, but none of the sources says whether that is enough for such devices, and we did not check whether the two lists download reliably in mainland China.

People who write their own code, run servers or use command-line tools on their computers need to update each runtime they use. Go's fix is in the standard library's crypto/x509 package, and because Go compiles the standard library into the executable, programs have to be rebuilt with the new version. Python's certifi is a separately installed package with its own copy in every virtual environment and container, so each copy needs updating. According to the explainer page, the curl, python3 and other commands built into macOS do not check revocation when reading /etc/ssl/cert.pem, and the file had not been updated as of 22 October.

OpenJDK's 21 October advisory says Java provided by operating system packages mostly uses the system certificates, so updating the system is enough. Java installed separately, along with the FreeBSD and Homebrew packages, needs to be updated directly.

Cloudflare's blog warns against switching off certificate validation to get rid of certificate errors that appear after updating. The explainer page provides test URLs signed by the affected intermediates, and a certificate error when connecting with curl means curl no longer trusts those certificates. Cloudflare's blog also notes that such a test speaks only for the program tested, and programs that validate certificates in other ways need to be checked separately.

Removing the root protects programs that do not read revocation information, at the cost of invalidating some legitimate sites' certificates as well. eMudhra estimated on the incident ticket that about 30,000 certificates need replacing, and its statement says the impact is limited to a single customer ecosystem in the United States. From CT data up to 21 October, Chrome counted on the ticket about 30,800 unexpired certificate entries under this root, 99.9% of them issued by two subordinate intermediates of Internet2 and InCommon. According to Google's blog, Chrome plans to remove the same root from the Chrome Root Store on the morning of 27 October Pacific Time, and is assessing whether to keep trusting eMudhra's other certificates.

The explainer page says Apple devices have blocked the certificates since 19 October and Microsoft platforms since 20 October. As of 22 October, we had not found announcements from either company. According to the Bugzilla incident ticket, eMudhra had not filed a formal incident report as of late on 21 October UTC. The formal report, eMudhra's answers to Chrome's questions on the ticket, and Chrome's decision on eMudhra's other certificates are the things to watch next.

item.title: User data Telegram handed over to US law enforcement
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: A newly filed US federal court record includes a letter in which Telegram provided a user's phone number, user ID and IP address under a court order. Since September 2024, Telegram's privacy policy has allowed it to hand over IP addresses and phone numbers in criminal cases involving violations of its Terms of Service, no longer only for terror suspects, and the clause has no regional limit. As of 20 October, we had not seen a public response from Telegram to the filing.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Telegram, Internet Archive, 404 Media

404 Media reported on 16 October that a newly filed document in a US federal court includes a letter from Telegram to US authorities, providing a user's phone number, user ID and IP address under a court order. According to CyberInsider, the letter is dated 4 September and was filed on 15 October in a criminal case in the US District Court for the Western District of Louisiana. The clause in Telegram's privacy policy on handing over IP addresses and phone numbers has no regional limit, so users outside the United States are subject to the same rules. As of 20 October, we had not seen a public response from Telegram to the filing.

404 Media's report is paywalled and we could read only its opening, and as of 20 October we could not find the court document itself, so the details of the letter come from CyberInsider's report. The IP address in the letter carries a timestamp in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) marking the account's last login. In the letter, Telegram describes the disclosure as voluntary and states that providing the data does not mean accepting US jurisdiction.

According to CyberInsider, the attachment contains only account and connection information and no message content, though that does not mean investigators obtained nothing else through other channels. The same report says Telegram usually needs a phone number to look up an account's non-public data. A username or numeric ID sometimes works when the account was previously actioned for content moderation, or when Telegram enabled additional logging after receiving a formal request. The letter does not say whether additional logging was enabled for this account.

Section 8.3 of Telegram's privacy policy, which we checked on 20 October, says that when Telegram receives a valid court order it first carries out a legal analysis and may disclose IP addresses and phone numbers to the relevant authorities. The order must confirm that the user is a suspect in a criminal case involving violations of Telegram's Terms of Service, and such disclosures are included in quarterly transparency reports. An archived copy of the page shows that before the change on 23 September 2024 the section covered only terror suspects and stated "So far, this has never happened".

Telegram's transparency reports are available only by querying an official bot from a Telegram account, and according to Meduza's explainer from October 2024, the bot returns data only for the country where the querying account is registered. 404 Media quoted the bot's reply in January 2025: from January to September 2024, Telegram fulfilled 14 US requests for IP addresses or phone numbers affecting 108 users, and 900 requests affecting 2,253 users over the full year. A crowdsourced dataset on GitHub, compiled from bot replies that users pasted in, lists 1,706 requests affecting 4,807 users for the United States in 2025. Telegram does not publish these figures on the web.

Perspective

According to Telegram's FAQ and privacy policy, both checked on 20 October, ordinary chats (cloud chats, including one-to-one chats and groups) are encrypted between the client and the server and stored on Telegram's servers. Secret Chats are end-to-end encrypted, meaning only the two participants' devices can decrypt them, and are not stored on the servers, only on the device each participant used to open the chat. The FAQ's section on data requests says the decryption keys for cloud chats are split across different jurisdictions, and that "To this day, we have disclosed 0 bytes of user messages to third parties, including governments". That section covers only message content, while the conditions for handing over IP addresses and phone numbers are in Section 8.3 of the privacy policy.

What Telegram provided in this letter was account data: a phone number, a user ID and an IP address. Section 5.2 of the privacy policy says that, for account security and to prevent spam and abuse, Telegram may collect IP addresses, the devices and apps used, and the history of username changes. Where collected, these records are kept for up to 12 months. Registering an account also requires a phone number.

We are a community based in Taiwan, where Article 77 of the Regulations for Administration of Mobile Broadband Businesses requires operators to record each subscriber's name, address and two identity document numbers, keep them for at least a year after the contract ends, and provide them when authorities make an inquiry under the law. From Section 8.3 of Telegram's privacy policy and this rule, we infer that once the number of an account registered with a Taiwanese number is handed over, Taiwanese authorities making an inquiry under the law can match the account to the subscriber.

Telegram does not publish country figures on the web, so the numbers for other places in Asia also come from the crowdsourced GitHub dataset, which counts requests for IP addresses or phone numbers that Telegram fulfilled. South Korea had 0 from January to September 2024, then 270 requests affecting 658 users from October to December 2024, and 2,101 requests affecting 5,454 users in 2025. Singapore had 4 requests affecting 4 users in 2024 and 14 affecting 16 in the first quarter of 2025, while Hong Kong and Japan appear only for January to September 2024, both at 0. Taiwan has no entry, though Meduza's October 2024 table lists it at 0 for January to September 2024, and we could not find figures for Taiwan, Hong Kong or Japan after September 2024, or for Singapore after the first quarter of 2025.

What a handed-over number can be matched to depends on what the carrier registered behind it, and the rules differ across Asia. In Hong Kong, under a regulation on SIM card registration that took effect on 1 September 2021, every SIM service plan and prepaid card has required real-name registration before activation since 1 March 2022, and individuals register their name in English and Chinese, date of birth, and Hong Kong identity card number with a copy of the card. In Singapore, the licence template that the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) issues to operators, which is not the text of a statute, requires them to register prepaid subscribers' name, address, identity document number and contact details and keep the register for at least 12 months after the service ends.

Article 32-4 of South Korea's Telecommunications Business Act, in the version in force from 1 October 2026, requires designated carriers to verify, with the subscriber's consent, that the person signing the contract is who they claim to be, and lets them ask for an identity card, including the mobile version, or a driver's licence. In Japan, Article 3 of the Act on Identity Confirmation by Mobile Voice Communications Carriers requires carriers to confirm an individual subscriber's name, address and date of birth at contract, and the 2026 White Paper on Information and Communications from the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications says the Act was amended in 2026 to require identity checks for data-only SIMs as well; we did not check when that amendment takes effect. We did not check whether the Korean and Japanese rules cover prepaid SIMs.

According to the FAQ, your phone number is visible by default only to people you have added to your own contacts, and the setting is under Settings > Privacy and Security > Phone Number. A 2019 post on Telegram's blog says that after setting who can see your number to Nobody, you can also limit who can find you by your number to your contacts (names in the current app may differ). According to the same post, strangers who add your number to their contacts then cannot match it to your profile, though the FAQ notes that people who already have your number saved can still see it. Usernames are always public, and the FAQ suggests not setting one if you do not want to be found through search.

For people who handle sensitive conversations, the FAQ recommends using Secret Chats with a self-destruct timer only in official or verifiable open-source apps, and turning on two-step verification and a passcode lock. To start a Secret Chat, open the other person's profile, tap "…" and choose Start Secret Chat, and note that Secret Chats disappear when you log out. Telegram's translation platform has a Traditional Chinese language pack that switches the interface through a share link, while the FAQ and privacy policy have no Chinese version. Our inference from Section 5.2 of the privacy policy and the phone number requirement at sign-up is that none of these steps means Telegram lacks the account's phone number, and whether IP addresses are collected depends on the circumstances described in Section 5.2.

item.title: Customer-list matching and conversation context in ChatGPT ads
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Advertisers on ChatGPT can upload lists of email addresses, phone numbers or mobile advertising IDs so that their ads reach only the people on those lists. Ads appear only on the Free and Go plans and began rolling out in Taiwan on 23 September. According to OpenAI's help page as of 20 October, ChatGPT still picks ads based on the current conversation after ad personalisation is turned off.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 15 sources, including OpenAI, 404 Media, Gizmodo

Advertisers on ChatGPT can upload lists of email addresses, phone numbers or mobile advertising IDs so that their ads are shown only to the people on those lists, 404 Media reported on 15 October. The feature appears on OpenAI's help page for advertisers under the name Custom Audiences. Ads appear only on the Free plan and the cheaper paid Go plan, not on Plus, Pro, Business or other plans, and began rolling out in Taiwan on 23 September. According to OpenAI's user help page as of 20 October, ChatGPT still picks ads based on the current conversation after ad personalisation is turned off.

According to the Custom Audiences help page, a list can contain email addresses, phone numbers, SHA-256 hashes of either, or Google Advertising IDs (GAID, the advertising identifier on Android phones). A hash is a one-way function that turns data into a fixed-length string. Advertisers can also upload raw, unhashed data, and uploaded files are usually deleted within 24 hours. OpenAI matches the list against ChatGPT users, and only the people matched count towards the audience.

A list can be used to show ads only to that audience, to exclude it, or to raise or lower the bid (what the advertiser is willing to pay for an impression or click) for it. Targeting an audience or adjusting bids requires at least 25,000 matched users, while an exclusion list can match fewer than 25,000. Ads Manager does not show which individuals were matched.

According to Gizmodo's account of the 404 Media report, 404 Media ran two ad campaigns on ChatGPT to test the system. Per the same account, it is unclear whether OpenAI hashes raw data after receiving it. The 404 Media report is paywalled, with only its first two paragraphs public, so the remaining details rely on Gizmodo's account.

According to OpenAI's user help page, OpenAI does not give advertisers users' conversations, memories, names, email addresses, precise location or IP addresses, and advertisers receive only aggregate performance figures such as views and clicks. If a user messages an advertiser through an ad, the advertiser can see those messages. Ads are not placed near conversations on sensitive topics such as personal health, mental health and politics, and are not shown in Temporary Chats or to accounts judged to belong to under-18s.

Perspective

Targeting ads with customer lists is common in the industry, and Google's Customer Match and Meta's customer list custom audiences are the same kind of feature. According to Meta's help page, Meta hashes a list before matching it, and according to Google's, Google does not receive the actual email addresses. The upload formats on OpenAI's help page include unhashed raw data. 404 Media also reported that ChatGPT ads are chosen based on the prompts users type.

Under OpenAI's Ad Tools Terms for advertisers, a list may contain only first-party data the advertiser collected itself, not data obtained from data brokers (companies that collect and resell personal data). Advertisers must warrant that they have given the required notice and obtained any necessary consent or other legal basis, and nothing in the terms describes how OpenAI verifies this. As of 20 October, the user help page has nothing on how to find out which advertisers' lists you are on. The ad menu has an "About this ad" option for seeing why a particular ad was shown, and the help page does not cover whether it reveals customer lists.

Our 26 September piece covered the pixel (tracking code advertisers install on their own sites), which sends browsing data from other sites back to OpenAI. Under OpenAI's privacy policy (the version for users outside the EEA, the UK and Switzerland), OpenAI may receive information from advertisers, such as purchases users make from them, and use it to show more relevant ads.

As of 20 October, mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau are not on OpenAI's list of countries and territories where ChatGPT is supported, nor on the list for its API. According to the ChatGPT list, using the service from outside the listed places may get an account blocked or suspended. ChatGPT ads began rolling out on 23 September in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam and Taiwan, following earlier Asia-Pacific launches in Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea and India. According to OpenAI's help page, personalised ads are initially unavailable in the European Economic Area and Switzerland, with no other exceptions named, so no Asian market is set apart in the same way.

Customer lists are built from data advertisers hold about their own customers, and the rules in the places we checked differ. Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act has no provision specifically on advertising identifiers, real-time bidding or targeted ads, and the Chinese word for advertising (廣告) does not appear in its text. Its Article 20 does require a non-government entity that markets with personal data to stop once the person objects, and to offer a way to object the first time it markets to them. We read only the statute itself as of 18 October, not its enforcement rules or regulators' interpretations, and amendments dated 11 November 2025 are to take effect on a date set by the Executive Yuan.

Japan amended its Telecommunications Business Act in June 2022. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications page, which we checked as of 18 October and which shows no update date, online information services such as messaging, social media, search and news that send user data to outside parties through tags or information-collection modules must give notice of or publish what is sent, or obtain consent or offer a way to stop it, though the rule does not ban targeted ads and does not cover corporate websites or personal blogs. South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission published a policy plan on 31 January 2024 to protect the online behavioural data used in targeted ads and set out to revise its targeted-advertising guidelines, though as of 18 October we could not find whether the revised guidelines are in force.

People on the Free or Go plan can go to Settings > Ad Controls in ChatGPT to turn off Personalize ads, and can also turn off Past chats and memory, a toggle that affects only ads. Ads data can be deleted in the same place, and is removed from OpenAI's servers within 30 days. According to the help page, people who cannot see these options in the mobile app should update it to the latest version. Turning off personalisation does not remove ads, and ChatGPT still picks them based on the current conversation.

People who do not want ads can switch to Plus or Pro, and the Free plan also has an ad-free option, though according to the help page its availability may vary by region and over time. The ad-free option comes with fewer messages per day and no access to tools such as image generation, and Go users have to switch back to Free to use it. In the Traditional Chinese version of the help page, the step "Change plan to go ad-free" appears as 「輕觸變更方案以享受 Go 無廣告體驗」, which reads as enjoying an ad-free Go plan, so follow the English wording. Because Temporary Chats do not show ads according to the help page, we infer that people who do not want a particular conversation to shape their ads can use a Temporary Chat.

Lists can contain email addresses, phone numbers and GAIDs, and as of 20 October OpenAI has not explained which account data it matches them against. If matching uses the email address and phone number registered to the ChatGPT account (our inference), a list built from a different address or number used for shopping or memberships may not match. Whether OpenAI will explain how it handles the raw data it receives, and whether turning off personalisation also excludes people from list matching, are the points to watch.

item.title: Implanted chips in Ledger hardware wallets
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 15 October Ledger confirmed that a criminal group had fitted genuine hardware wallets with parts that capture the recovery phrase during setup, then put them on the market through resellers in Southeast Asia. As of 13 October, the thefts Ledger had confirmed were all tied to devices sold by authorised reseller CryptoBilis, and reports of implants from other channels were unconfirmed. Ledger's Genuine Check cannot detect these implants, and Ledger advises anyone who bought and set up a device from CryptoBilis to move their assets to a new device and a new recovery phrase.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 20 sources, including Ledger, Ledger Support, Ledger Academy

Hardware wallet maker Ledger confirmed on its official blog on 15 October that a criminal group had spent months buying genuine Ledger devices. The group opened them and fitted hidden components that capture the recovery phrase (24 English words that can restore everything in the wallet) while the user sets the device up, then put the devices back on the market through resellers in Southeast Asia. According to the timeline from on-chain analytics firm Bitquery, the mass thefts began on 9 October. According to The Record, citing Ledger's 13 October statement, all confirmed thefts are linked to devices sold by CryptoBilis, an authorised Ledger reseller in Southeast Asia.

Cointelegraph reported that Ledger also said on 13 October it had not confirmed thefts from devices bought through other channels. Ledger's 15 October post says it has asked resellers in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to pause sales. Ledger's Genuine Check, which connects to Ledger's servers to confirm that the secure element is original, cannot detect implants of this kind.

Ledger's 15 October post says there is no flaw in its chips, operating system or servers. In the post, Ledger describes the incident as a "localized distribution attack" that took place in the distribution channel after the devices left Ledger, and The Record also cites Ledger as saying the number of affected devices is limited. According to The Record, citing Ledger's 13 October statement, the implant reads what is shown on the screen, picks out the recovery phrase during setup and sends it out over the LTE mobile network through a built-in eSIM.

Tibane Labs, a blockchain research and development company, took apart two Nano X units bought from a Japanese auction site and a seller on Amazon Japan, and its page states that it did not test any CryptoBilis devices. The implant is a small computer soldered to the main board and wired to the screen's data line, and it makes no attempt to break the secure element (the chip that stores the private keys). Tibane Labs compared three versions and found that the dedicated antenna on the latest one is printed with a part number and version number, from which it inferred that the implant is mass-produced.

As of 20 October, Ledger has not disclosed the affected models, batches, number of people or amounts. Bitquery counted 335 wallets and US$102 million drained as of 16 October, and the US$92.9 million in earlier reports from crypto.news and others was an earlier Bitquery figure. Bitquery's page says the on-chain record points to a single actor holding the keys to every drained wallet, but the chain shows only transfers, not where the keys leaked from.

Zero Day, a security journalist's newsletter, reported on 13 October on claims of implants in devices bought outside CryptoBilis. An unnamed Japanese researcher told Zero Day he had bought ten units in total from unauthorised online sellers, the earliest in March, and every one had an implant. The same report cites a post on X by a German buyer who said he bought implanted Nano X units from MediaMarkt, which Ledger lists as an authorised reseller in Germany, at two of its stores. As of 20 October, Ledger has not confirmed these accounts.

The Record quotes Ledger's 13 October statement as saying it is "also reviewing reports of implants in other signers and locations". According to crypto.news, MediaMarkt paused sales with Ledger's agreement. Ledger said it had received no reports of lost funds in the German cases and had not established whether the German reports were related to the others. Ledger's 15 October post says it sent people to buy and open devices in markets including Germany and that "Every unit examined was clean", without giving the number of units examined.

Perspective

According to Ledger's educational site Ledger Academy, the private keys are stored in the secure element. The device generates the recovery phrase at initialisation and displays it only that once. Ledger's support page on checking hardware integrity says Genuine Check verifies a key written into the secure element at the factory, which keeps out counterfeits. The same page notes that as long as the original secure element is intact, Genuine Check cannot detect physical modifications such as implants.

The implant described by The Record and Tibane Labs leaves the secure element alone and reads the recovery phrase off the screen's data line at the moment it is displayed. The hardware integrity page says that on the Nano X and Nano S Plus, the secure element checks the main microcontroller's firmware at startup and shows a warning if it has been altered. The other check the page lists is opening the case and comparing the inside with Ledger's official photos to make sure no extra chip has been added. Tibane Labs' page says the device itself cannot detect the implant, and that the latest version is painted the same colour as the original circuit board.

According to The Record, citing Ledger's 13 October statement, anyone with a CryptoBilis device that has not been set up should leave it that way and contact support. Those who have already set one up should move their assets to a new device and a new recovery phrase as soon as possible, and should not enter or restore any recovery phrase on a device bought from CryptoBilis. Victims should contact Ledger and local police before deciding whether to open the device or send it anywhere.

For people who bought a Nano X of unknown origin through other channels and have already set it up, Ledger had made no recommendation to change the recovery phrase as of 20 October. Tibane Labs' page recommends replacing any recovery phrase that was shown on a Nano X of unknown origin, generating a new one on a trusted device and moving the assets to it. The page also says a recovery phrase shown on a modified screen should be treated as leaked even if the device has never been online. According to the hardware integrity page, people comfortable with hardware can open the case and compare, but damage from opening it is not covered by the warranty.

People who have not bought a device yet, or have just received one, can follow the purchasing guidance on Ledger's support site. Do not use a device whose packaging looks opened or resealed, or that comes with a card already filled in with a recovery phrase, and contact support instead. Ledger recommends buying from its official store or an authorised reseller, and as of 20 October its reseller page lists six resellers in Taiwan and five in Hong Kong, with no pause marked on the Hong Kong entries. These support pages had no Traditional Chinese version as of 20 October.

Elsewhere in Asia, the same reseller page lists six resellers in Singapore, only Amazon Japan for Japan, and no entry for mainland China. As of 20 October it marks "Sales temporarily paused" only on CryptoBilis in Indonesia and Malaysia and on some online shops in Malaysia and the Philippines. According to Cointelegraph, which reported a social media post from Ledger, the 13 October request covered resellers in Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Hong Kong, but the Hong Kong and Singapore entries carry no pause label. As of 20 October, Ledger's list of official Amazon stores includes Japan and Singapore but not Taiwan, Hong Kong or mainland China.

The crypto rules we found in Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China, Japan and Singapore concern service providers, trading platforms or crypto businesses, and as of 20 October we found no provision on selling, importing or owning hardware wallets themselves (which does not mean none exists). Taiwan's Virtual Asset Service Act, passed by the Legislative Yuan on 30 June 2026 with a start date still to be set by the Executive Yuan, covers seven kinds of virtual asset service providers, including exchanges, trading platforms, transfer services and custodians. The press release from the Securities and Futures Bureau of the Financial Supervisory Commission does not mention wallets or self-custody.

Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) requires centralised virtual asset trading platforms doing business in Hong Kong or marketing to Hong Kong investors to be licensed, and its page does not mention wallets. The 2020 English translation of Japan's Payment Services Act counts managing crypto-assets on behalf of another person as a crypto-asset exchange service; we did not check later amendments, and the translation does not mention wallets. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) brought custody of digital payment tokens under its Payment Services Act from April 2024, and its page does not mention wallets either.

In mainland China, eight departments including the People's Bank of China issued a notice on further preventing and dealing with risks related to virtual currency on 6 February 2026. We read only a media reprint of its full text, which treats domestic virtual currency exchange and trading as suspected illegal financial activity and says that civil acts of investing in virtual currency that violate public order and good morals are void, but it does not mention wallets.

CryptoBilis and MediaMarkt are both on Ledger's list of authorised resellers, and Ledger Academy's buying guide says "no global supply chain is entirely immune". Our inference is that buying through authorised channels lowers the risk but cannot guarantee a device has not been tampered with.

What comes of these two, and whether Ledger widens the scope of what it has confirmed, are the things to watch next.
